t: You made us for Yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in You.
x: We were made for God, so no job, success or relationship can satisfy us until we find our rest in him.

t: Too late I loved You, O Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new!
x: God's beauty is ancient yet always fresh; it is never too late to turn to him, and regret over lost years can fuel love.

t: Give what You command, and command what You will.
x: God never asks us to obey in our own strength; we can pray for the very grace to do what he commands.

t: Blessed is the one who loves You, and his friend in You, and his enemy for Your sake.
x: Loving God reorders every relationship, so we love friends in him and even enemies for his sake.

t: Accordingly, two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self.
w: The City of God, Book 14, Chapter 28 (Dods translation)
x: Every life, home and institution is shaped by its deepest love: love of self pushes God out, love of God puts self in its place.

t: Our wisdom, in so far as it ought to be deemed true and solid Wisdom, consists almost entirely of two parts: the knowledge of God and of ourselves.
w: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 1, Chapter 1, Section 1 (Beveridge translation)
x: True wisdom starts with knowing God and knowing ourselves honestly; each sharpens the other and keeps us humble.

t: We are not our own; therefore, as far as possible, let us forget ourselves and the things that are ours. On the other hand, we are God's; let us, therefore, live and die to him.
w: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 3, Chapter 7, Section 1 (Beveridge translation)
x: Belonging to God frees us from living for ourselves; our time, gifts and plans are his to direct, in life and death.

t: Hence we may infer, that the human mind is, so to speak, a perpetual forge of idols.
w: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 1, Chapter 11, Section 8 (Beveridge translation)
x: Our hearts constantly manufacture substitutes for God, so we must keep watching what we really trust and love most.

t: There is no work so mean and so sordid that does not look truly respectable and highly important in the sight of God.
w: Golden Booklet of the True Christian Life (1551; van Andel translation), p. 94
x: Ordinary, unseen work done in God's calling has real dignity before him, from the classroom to the kitchen.

t: Being humbled, we learn to call upon his strength which alone makes us stand up under such a load of afflictions.
w: Golden Booklet of the True Christian Life (1551; van Andel translation), p. 50
x: Hardship strips away self-reliance and teaches us to lean on God's strength, which alone can carry us through.

t: Faith is a living, daring confidence in God's grace, so sure and certain that a man would stake his life on it a thousand times.
w: Preface to the Epistle to the Romans (1522; Luther's Works vol. 35)
x: Faith is not a vague feeling but bold trust in God's grace, strong enough to stake everything on it.

t: That now, I say, upon which you set your heart and put your trust is properly your god.
x: Whatever we most rely on for security and meaning functions as our god, so our trust reveals our true worship.

t: The true treasure of the Church is the Most Holy Gospel of the glory and the grace of God.
w: Ninety-Five Theses (1517), Thesis 62 (Works of Martin Luther, 1915)
x: The church's greatest wealth is the gospel of God's grace, not its buildings, programs or reputation.

t: Our Lord and Master Jesus Christ, when He said Poenitentiam agite, willed that the whole life of believers should be repentance.
w: Ninety-Five Theses (1517), Thesis 1 (Works of Martin Luther, 1915)
x: Repentance is not a one-time event but the daily pattern of the Christian life, turning again and again to Christ.

t: There is no more lovely, friendly and charming relationship, communion or company than a good marriage.
x: A good marriage is one of God's richest gifts, a friendship and companionship worth cherishing and protecting.

t: Resolved, to live with all my might, while I do live.
x: Life is short and given by God, so we should give ourselves wholeheartedly to every day and every task.

t: Resolved, never to lose one moment of time, but to improve it in the most profitable way I possibly can.
x: Time is a trust from God; using it well, rather than drifting, is part of faithful stewardship.

t: Resolved, never to do any thing, which I should be afraid to do if it were the last hour of my life.
x: Living as if this were our last hour keeps us from actions we would be ashamed to bring before God.

t: Resolved, never to give over, nor in the least to slacken, my fight with my corruptions, however unsuccessful I may be.
x: Faithfulness means refusing to quit the fight against sin, even when progress seems slow or invisible.

t: True religion, in great part, consists in holy affections.
x: Real faith engages the heart, not just the head; love, joy and hope toward God lie at the core of true religion.

t: Care more for a grain of faith than a ton of excitement.
w: Lectures to My Students, First Series, Lecture 11
x: Quiet, genuine trust in God matters far more than emotional highs or outward enthusiasm in ministry and life.

t: My trust is not that I am holy, but that, being unholy, Christ died for me.
w: As quoted in Gilbert, Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895), p. 592
x: Our confidence before God rests on Christ's death for sinners, not on our own performance or goodness.

t: I would rather go to Heaven doubting all the way than be lost through self-confidence.
x: Humble, wrestling faith is safer than proud self-assurance; complacency is a greater danger than honest doubt.

t: Losses and crosses are heavy to bear; but when our hearts are right with God, it is wonderful how easy the yoke becomes.
w: As quoted in Gilbert, Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895), p. 169
x: Suffering is real and heavy, but a heart at peace with God finds Christ's yoke surprisingly light.

t: Jesus was a great worker, and His disciples must not be afraid of hard work.
w: As quoted in Gilbert, Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895), p. 128
x: Christ worked tirelessly for others, so his followers should embrace hard work as part of serving him.

t: The Christian ideal has not been tried and found wanting. It has been found difficult; and left untried.
w: What's Wrong with the World, Part 1, Chapter 5, "The Unfinished Temple"
x: Christianity's failures usually come from not attempting its hard demands, not from the faith itself falling short.

t: Joy, which was the small publicity of the pagan, is the gigantic secret of the Christian.
x: Christian joy runs deeper than worldly cheer; beneath real sorrows lies a settled gladness rooted in God.

t: Angels can fly because they can take themselves lightly.
x: Humility and not taking ourselves too seriously bring freedom and lightness; pride weighs the soul down.

t: I would maintain that thanks are the highest form of thought; and that gratitude is happiness doubled by wonder.
w: A Short History of England (1917), p. 59
x: Gratitude joined with wonder multiplies joy; giving thanks is the fitting response to every gift from God.

t: The world will never starve for want of wonders; but only for want of wonder.
x: The world is full of God's wonders; what we lack is the attentive, grateful eyes to notice them.

t: Aim at Heaven and you will get earth 'thrown in': aim at earth and you will get neither.
x: When we seek God first, earthly goods fall into their proper place; chasing earthly things alone loses both.

t: God whispers to us in our pleasures, speaks in our conscience, but shouts in our pains: it is His megaphone to rouse a deaf world.
w: The Problem of Pain, Chapter 6, "Human Pain"
x: God can use pain to wake us from complacency and draw us to himself when gentler means go unheard.

t: There are no ordinary people. You have never talked to a mere mortal.
w: "The Weight of Glory" (1941 sermon), in The Weight of Glory and Other Addresses
x: Every person we meet is an eternal being, which should shape how we teach, lead and treat others.

t: To love at all is to be vulnerable. Love anything, and your heart will certainly be wrung and possibly be broken.
x: Real love always risks hurt; refusing to love in order to stay safe slowly hardens the heart.

t: Every Christian is to become a little Christ.
x: The goal of the Christian life is to be shaped into Christ's likeness, sharing his life with the world.

t: Gratitude looks to the past and love to the present; fear, avarice, lust, and ambition look ahead.
x: Gratitude and love keep us grounded in what God has done and is doing, while anxious ambition lives in the future.

t: Cheap grace is the deadly enemy of our Church. We are fighting to-day for costly grace.
w: The Cost of Discipleship (1937; English tr. 1959), p. 43
x: Grace is free but never cheap; it calls us to follow Christ wholeheartedly rather than excuse ongoing sin.

t: Suffering willingly endured is stronger than evil, it spells death to evil.
x: Patiently bearing wrong, as Christ did, overcomes evil instead of feeding it with retaliation.

t: Time is the most precious gift in our possession, for it is the most irrevocable.
w: Letters and Papers from Prison, p. 47
x: Time cannot be recovered once spent, so every hour deserves careful stewardship before God.

t: We are to find God in what we know, not in what we don't know.
w: Letters and Papers from Prison, letter to Eberhard Bethge, 25 May 1944
x: God is not just a filler for gaps in our knowledge; he is Lord over all of life, including what we understand.

t: Prayer will consume sin, or sin will choke prayer.
x: Prayer and willful sin cannot coexist for long; one will drive out the other, so guard your prayer life.

t: Knowledge of the Bible never comes by intuition. It can only be got by hard, regular, daily, attentive, wakeful reading.
w: Expository Thoughts on the Gospels: St. Matthew, on Matthew 4:1-11
x: Biblical understanding grows through steady, disciplined daily reading, not shortcuts or sudden insight.

t: Ignorance of Scripture is the root of every error in religion, and the source of every heresy.
w: Expository Thoughts on the Gospels: St. John, Vol. 1, Preface
x: Most spiritual error grows from not knowing the Bible well, which is why teaching Scripture matters so much.

t: The heart is the part of man which God chiefly notices in religion.
w: Expository Thoughts on the Gospels: St. Mark, on Mark 7:1-13
x: God looks past outward religion to the heart, so our inner motives matter more than appearances.

t: The parent who tries to train without setting a good example is building with one hand and pulling down with the other.
w: The Upper Room, Chapter 16, "The Duties of Parents"
x: Children learn more from what parents do than what they say; a godly example must match godly instruction.

t: Put sin to death; make it your daily work; keep at it as long as you live; do not stop for a single day; be killing sin or it will be killing you.
w: Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers, Chapter 2 (modernized)
x: Fighting sin is a daily, lifelong task; if we stop resisting it, sin will quietly destroy our spiritual life.

t: Let no one think he is making any progress in holiness if he does not walk over the bellies of his lusts.
w: Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers, Chapter 2 (modernized)
x: Real growth in holiness requires actively defeating sinful desires, not merely admiring good ideals.

t: Watch yourselves, in case your example contradicts your teaching ... in case you undo with your lives what you say with your tongues.
x: Leaders must make sure their lives back up their words, or their example will undo their teaching.

t: Whoever means what he says will surely do what he says.
x: Sincerity shows itself in action; if we truly mean what we say, our deeds will follow our words.

t: The essence of the Christian religion consists in the reality that the creation of the Father, ruined by sin, is restored in the death of the Son of God and re-created by the grace of the Holy Spirit into a kingdom of God.
x: The gospel is God's plan to restore his whole creation through Christ and the Spirit, giving all of life purpose.

t: Your best servant is the one who is not so eager to hear from You what he himself wants, as to want what he hears from You.
x: Mature prayer seeks to want what God wills rather than to get God to approve what we already want.

t: Bad times, hard times, this is what people keep saying; but let us live well, and times shall be good. We are the times: Such as we are, such are the times.
x: Instead of blaming the age, Christians shape their times by how faithfully they live in their homes, schools and work.

t: Since you cannot do good to all, you are to pay special regard to those who, by the accidents of time, or place, or circumstance, are brought into closer connection with you.
x: We cannot help everyone, so God's providence points our love first to the family, students and neighbours he has placed near us.

t: What is love's perfection? To love our enemies, and to love them to the end that they may be our brothers.
w: Ten Homilies on the First Epistle of John, Homily 1 (Burnaby translation)
x: Christian love aims beyond tolerating opponents; it seeks their good and hopes to see them reconciled as brothers in Christ.

t: Let this be our rule for goodwill and helpfulness, that whenever we are able to assist others we should behave as stewards who must someday give an account of ourselves.
w: Golden Booklet of the True Christian Life (1551; van Andel translation), p. 35
x: Our abilities, money and time are on loan from God, so helping others is a duty we will answer for, not an optional kindness.

t: We should forever keep in mind that we must not brood on the wickedness of man, but realize that he is God's image bearer.
w: Golden Booklet of the True Christian Life (1551; van Andel translation), p. 38
x: Seeing God's image in difficult people, including students and colleagues, frees us to treat them with respect instead of contempt.

t: A Christian ought to be disposed and prepared to keep in mind that he has to reckon with God every moment of his life.
w: Golden Booklet of the True Christian Life (1551; van Andel translation), p. 28
x: Living before God's face in every moment, not just on Sundays, brings integrity to private choices and public work alike.

t: Since God has revealed himself as a Father, we would be guilty of the basest ingratitude if we did not behave as his children.
w: Golden Booklet of the True Christian Life (1551; van Andel translation), p. 19
x: Holy living flows from gratitude: those adopted by a loving Father want to reflect his character as his children.

t: We do not become righteous by doing righteous deeds but, having been made righteous, we do righteous deeds.
x: Good works do not earn God's favour; they grow out of the righteousness God freely gives, which removes both pride and despair.

t: For what must be enforced with rods and blows only will not develop into a good breed, and at best they will remain godly under such treatment no longer than while the rod is upon their back.
w: Large Catechism, The Second Commandment (Bente translation)
x: Children and students formed only by fear obey only while watched; lasting godliness is nurtured with kindness and the fear of God.

t: Mother love is stronger than the filth and scabbiness on a child, and so the love of God toward us is stronger than the dirt that clings to us.
x: As a parent loves a messy child, God's love for his people is greater than their sin, which should shape how we love our own children.

t: Resolved, to ask myself, at the end of every day, week, month, and year, wherein I could possibly, in any respect, have done better.
x: Regular honest self-review, done before God, turns ordinary days into steady growth in character, work and leadership.

t: Resolved, that I will live so, as I shall wish I had done when I come to die.
x: Remembering our deathbed clarifies today's priorities, putting faith, family and faithfulness ahead of passing concerns.

t: Let there be something of benevolence in all that I speak.
x: Our words, at home, in class and in meetings, should always carry goodwill toward others, even when they must correct or confront.

t: The practice of truth is the most profitable reading of it.
w: Morning and Evening, entry for June 20
x: Scripture does us the most good when we obey it; knowing the Bible without living it misses its purpose.

t: If you tell your troubles to God, you put them into the grave; they will never rise again when you have committed them to Him. If you roll your burden anywhere else, it will roll back again like the stone of Sisyphus.
w: As quoted in Gilbert, Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895), p. 596
x: Worry and complaint only bring our burdens back; prayer hands them to the one who can actually carry them.

t: The truest lengthening of life is to live while we live, wasting no time but using every hour for the highest ends. So be it this day.
x: A full life is measured by how well its hours are spent for God, not by its length, so today is the day to live purposefully.

t: Tradition means giving votes to the most obscure of all classes, our ancestors. It is the democracy of the dead.
x: Wise leaders and teachers listen to the faithful generations before them instead of assuming the present always knows best.

t: Courage is almost a contradiction in terms. It means a strong desire to live taking the form of a readiness to die.
x: Echoing Christ's call to lose life to save it, true courage holds life dear yet is willing to lay it down for what is right.

t: The Bible tells us to love our neighbors, and also to love our enemies; probably because they are generally the same people.
x: The hardest people to love are often the ones closest to us, so Christ's command to love enemies starts at home and work.

t: I believe in Christianity as I believe that the sun has risen. Not only because I see it, but because by it I see everything else.
w: "Is Theology Poetry?" (1945 address to the Oxford Socratic Club)
x: Christianity is not just one belief among many but the light that makes sense of all of life, learning and work.

t: A proud man is always looking down on things and people: and, of course, as long as you are looking down, you cannot see something that is above you.
w: Mere Christianity, Book 3, Chapter 8, "The Great Sin"
x: Pride blinds us to God; looking down on others keeps us from looking up to the one who is above us all.

t: If I find in myself a desire which no experience in this world can satisfy, the most probable explanation is that I was made for another world.
x: Our unsatisfied longings point beyond this life to God and heaven, freeing us from demanding that earthly things fill us completely.

t: The hardness of God is kinder than the softness of men, and His compulsion is our liberation.
x: When God presses hard on us, it is for our freedom and good, unlike indulgent human kindness that leaves us unchanged.

t: God cannot give us a happiness and peace apart from Himself, because it is not there. There is no such thing.
w: Mere Christianity, Book 2, Chapter 3, "The Shocking Alternative"
x: Lasting peace is found only in God himself, so seeking happiness anywhere else, even in good gifts, will always fall short.

t: We must be ready to allow ourselves to be interrupted by God. God will be constantly crossing our paths and canceling our plans by sending us people with claims and petitions.
x: The child, student or colleague who interrupts our plans may be God's assignment for the day, not an obstacle to our real work.

t: It is not your love that sustains the marriage, but from now on, the marriage that sustains your love.
w: Letters and Papers from Prison, "A Wedding Sermon from a Prison Cell" (May 1943)
x: Marriage is a covenant God establishes, and keeping its promises carries a couple through seasons when feelings run low.

t: The will of God, to which the law gives expression, is that men should defeat their enemies by loving them.
w: The Cost of Discipleship, "The Enemy, the Extraordinary", p. 147
x: Christians overcome hostility not by retaliation but by active love, which is the costly way Christ defeated his own enemies.

t: Christians may not permit their conduct to be determined by the spirit of the age, but must focus on the requirement of God's commandment
x: Families and schools are shaped by cultural trends, but Christians take their direction from God's word, not the mood of the moment.

t: The history of the human race begins with a wedding
x: God himself established marriage at the start of history, giving husbands and wives a calling central to his purposes for the world.

t: The world's idea of greatness is to rule, but Christian greatness consists in serving.
w: Expository Thoughts on the Gospels: St. Mark, on Mark 9:30-37
x: Christ redefines leadership: the greatest in his kingdom are those who serve others, not those who hold the most power.

t: Our Lord has many weak children in His family, many dull pupils in His school, many raw soldiers in His army, and many lame sheep in His flock. Yet He bears with them all, and casts none away.
w: Expository Thoughts on the Gospels: St. John, Vol. 3, on John 20:24-31
x: Christ's patience with slow, struggling disciples comforts us and models how teachers and parents should bear with those in their care.

t: The Bible in the pulpit must never supersede the Bible at home.
x: Good preaching cannot replace a father's and mother's own reading and teaching of Scripture in the home.

t: Fear puts an end to openness of manner; fear leads to concealment; fear sows the seed of much hypocrisy, and leads to many a lie.
w: The Upper Room, Chapter 16, "The Duties of Parents"
x: Children ruled by fear learn to hide and pretend, so parents and teachers should lead with love that invites honesty.

t: Sin always aims at the utmost; every time it rises up to tempt or entice, if it had its own way, it would go to the very worst sin of that kind.
w: Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers, Chapter 2 (modernized)
x: Small sins are never harmless, because every temptation aims at full ruin; wisdom deals with them early and seriously.

t: Indeed, just as your great worry is about the Father's love, so there is no way you can trouble or burden him more than by unkindly refusing to believe in it.
w: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, Part 1, Chapter 3 (modernized)
x: Doubting the Father's love grieves him; believers honour God by resting in his love rather than questioning it.

t: Many a tailor goes about in rags while making costly clothes for others; and many a cook barely licks his fingers after preparing the most costly dishes for others.
x: Those who feed others spiritually, as pastors, teachers and parents, can starve their own souls; we must take the truth we give.

t: Do not be content with being in a state of grace, but take care also that your graces are kept in vigorous, lively exercise, and that you preach to yourselves the sermons you study before you preach them to others.
x: Anyone who teaches others must first apply the lesson to their own heart, keeping their faith active rather than merely professional.

t: God never saved any man for being a preacher, nor because he was an able preacher; but because he was a justified, sanctified man, and consequently faithful in his Master's work.
x: Gifts and positions do not make us right with God; only grace does, and faithful service flows from that grace.

t: The two great graces essential to a saint in this life are faith and repentance. These are the two wings by which he flies to heaven.
x: Trusting Christ and turning from sin belong together; the Christian life needs both, as a bird needs two wings.

t: Our work is great, our time short, our Master urgent.
w: The Christian Soldier; or Heaven Taken by Storm (1669)
x: With much to do for God and limited time, believers should pursue their calling with focus and earnestness.

t: Nothing can hurt the soul but sin. Affliction does not hurt it; it often makes it better, as the furnace makes gold purer. It is sin that does the damage.
w: A Body of Divinity (1692), "Christ the Redeemer" (modernized)
x: Hardship can refine us like gold in a furnace; the real danger to the soul is sin, not suffering.

t: He that is down, needs fear no fall; / He that is low, no pride: / He that is humble, ever shall / Have God to be his guide.
w: The Pilgrim's Progress, Part 2 (the shepherd boy's song)
x: Humility brings security and contentment, because God guides those who do not trust in their own height.

t: My sword I give to him that shall succeed me in my pilgrimage, and my courage and skill to him that can get it.
x: Faithful believers pass on their tools and example to the next generation, who must then earn courage and skill for themselves.

t: The soul of religion is the practical part.
w: The Pilgrim's Progress, Part 1 (Christian on Talkative)
x: Talking well about faith is empty without obedience; genuine religion shows itself in how we actually live.

t: Precepts may instruct, but examples persuade.
x: Parents, teachers and leaders shape others most by how they live, so their example must reinforce their words.

t: An excellent master is always better than an excellent law. Let your laws be ever so good, if the lawmakers are bad, all will come to nothing.
x: Good rules and systems cannot replace godly character in those who lead; leaders' integrity matters more than policies.

t: The lives of such are most desirable, and the deaths of such will be most lamented, who make it their business to serve their generation.
x: A life spent serving the people of our own day for God's sake is the kind most valued and most missed.

t: ... not made out of his head to rule over him, nor out of his feet to be trampled upon by him, but out of his side to be equal with him, under his arm to be protected, and near his heart to be beloved.
w: Commentary on the Whole Bible, on Genesis 2:21
x: A husband is called to honour, protect and cherish his wife as his equal and beloved partner, never to dominate or demean her.

t: Whatever we have, the property of it is God's; we have only the use of it, according to the direction of our great Lord, and for his honour.
w: Commentary on the Whole Bible, on Luke 16
x: We are managers, not owners, of everything we have, so money, time and talents should be used as God directs and for his glory.

t: Extraordinary afflictions are not always the punishment of extraordinary sins, but sometimes the trial of extraordinary graces.
w: As quoted in Gilbert, Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895), p. 9
x: Severe suffering is not proof of God's anger; like Job's trials, it may be God strengthening and displaying deep faith.

t: His death there on Calvary's cross is for us individually, but it's not egotistically individualistic. Our individual salvation will one day be a portion of the restoration of all things.
w: "A Christian Manifesto" (1982 lecture, Coral Ridge Presbyterian Church)
x: Personal salvation is part of God's plan to renew all creation, which gives meaning to Christian work for healing in every area of life.

t: A leader is one who knows the way, goes the way, and shows the way.
x: People follow someone who has walked the road first, so lead by going ahead and helping others see the next step.

t: Leadership is not about titles, positions, or flowcharts. It is about one life influencing another.
x: Influence grows from relationships, not rank, so you can lead well in a classroom, a staff room, or at home.

t: All great achievers are given multiple reasons to believe they are failures. But in spite of that they persevere.
x: Feeling like a failure is normal on the way to anything worthwhile; what matters is choosing to keep going.

t: The best leaders are those who understand that their power comes not from their position, but from their ability to empower others.
x: Real strength in leadership shows when you help others grow in skill and confidence, not when you hold control.

t: The greatest danger to most organizations is not external threats, but internal weaknesses.
x: Most teams are hurt more by unaddressed problems inside than by pressure outside, so tend your own house first.

t: The bottom line in leadership isn't how far we advance ourselves but how far we advance others.
x: Measure your leadership by how much the people around you grow, not by how far you personally get ahead.

t: If you want to be a leader, the good news is that you can do it. Everyone has the potential, but it isn't accomplished overnight.
x: Leadership can be learned by anyone, but it grows slowly through steady practice rather than a single big moment.

t: Every message that people receive is filtered through the messenger who delivers it.
x: People judge what you say by how far they trust you, so credibility has to be built before a message can land.

t: Great leaders always seem to embody two seemingly dissonant qualities: they are highly visionary and highly practical.
x: Good leaders hold a clear picture of the future and also do the practical work needed to get there.

t: When people respect you as a person, they admire you. When they respect you as a friend, they love you. When they respect you as a leader, they follow you.
x: Being liked and admired is good, but people follow those whose leadership they have come to respect.

t: Your values are the soul of your leadership, and they drive your behavior.
x: What you truly value shapes how you act every day, so clear, good values keep your leadership steady.

t: Everything rises and falls on leadership.
x: The health of any team, school, or family depends heavily on the quality of the person leading it.

t: Leadership is influence. Nothing more, nothing less.
x: Leadership is about how much you shape others' thinking and actions, whatever your title or role.

t: What happens to me doesn't have to determine what happens within me.
x: You can't control every hard event, but you can choose your response and the kind of person it makes you.

t: How well you lead determines how well you succeed.
x: Your results usually track your leadership, so growing as a leader is one of the best investments you can make.

t: Good management of bad experiences leads to great personal growth.
x: Hard seasons can make you wiser if you reflect on them honestly instead of just trying to get past them.

t: We teach what we know, but we reproduce who we are.
x: People pick up your character more than your instructions, so who you are matters as much as what you say.

t: Great leaders reproduce great people because of who they are, not because of what they say.
x: Those you lead tend to become like you, so your example shapes the next generation of leaders.

t: There's no such thing as leadership by proxy.
x: You can delegate tasks, but not your example or presence; leadership has to be shown in person.

t: My greatest daily challenge is leading me.
x: Before you can lead others well, you have to manage your own attitude, habits, and choices each day.

t: When you stop loving people, you should stop leading people because you'll take advantage of them.
x: Leadership without care for people slides into using them, so love has to stay at the center of leading.

t: We are people of value who value people and add value to them.
x: Seeing people as valuable and working to add value to their lives is the heart of serving others well.

t: You cannot value others if you don't value yourself.
x: Healthy leaders accept their own worth, which frees them to honor and invest in other people.

t: People change when they hurt enough that they have to change, learn enough that they want to change, receive enough that they are able to change.
x: Growth comes through pain, learning, and support, so leaders help by teaching and resourcing, not just pushing.

t: Sometimes the seeds you sow take a long time to grow. But you always see a harvest.
x: Investing in people, students, or children often pays off slowly, so faithfulness matters more than quick results.

t: Growth is our only guarantee that tomorrow will get better.
x: You can't control tomorrow's circumstances, but steady personal growth makes you better ready to meet them.

t: Leaders hate change as much as followers, unless the change is their idea.
x: Even leaders resist change they didn't choose, so bring people into decisions if you want them to embrace change.

t: The pace of the leader determines the pace of the people.
x: Teams rarely move faster or work harder than the person leading them, so set the pace you hope others will keep.

t: Leaders continue to lead if they continue to grow.
x: Your ability to keep leading depends on your willingness to keep learning and growing.

t: Leaders are like thermostats, not thermometers.
x: Good leaders set the emotional climate of a room or home rather than simply reacting to the mood around them.

t: Winning teams have players who make things happen.
x: Strong teams need people who take initiative and act, not just people who wait to be told what to do.

t: Leadership ability is the lid that determines a person's level of effectiveness.
x: Your capacity to lead caps how much you and your team can accomplish, so raising it lifts everything else.

t: Whatever you will accomplish is restricted by your ability to lead others.
x: Big goals usually need other people, so your results are limited by how well you can lead them.

t: People buy into the leader before they buy into the vision.
x: People commit to a person they trust before they commit to a plan, so build trust before casting vision.

t: A leader's courage has great value: it gives followers hope.
x: When a leader faces difficulty bravely, the people watching gain hope that they can face it too.

t: Followers are attracted to people who are better leaders than themselves.
x: People naturally look for leaders stronger than themselves, so growing your own leadership draws good people.

t: Become the kind of leader that people would follow voluntarily; even if you had no title or position.
w: The Great Big Book of Wisdom
x: If people would follow you even without your title, your leadership rests on character and trust, not authority.

t: Leadership is the ability to get extraordinary achievement from ordinary people.
x: Good leaders bring out unusual effort and results in normal people by believing in them and organizing them well.

t: Integrity is the most valuable and respected quality of leadership. Always keep your word.
x: Keeping your word, even in small things, builds the trust that every other part of leadership depends on.

t: Superior leaders are willing to admit a mistake and cut their losses. Be willing to admit that you've changed your mind. Don't persist when the original decision turns out to be a poor one.
x: Admitting a mistake and changing course shows strength and protects those you lead from a bad decision.

t: The glue that holds all relationships together–including the relationship between the leader and the led–is trust, and trust is based on integrity.
x: Trust holds every relationship together, at work and at home, and trust grows only from consistent integrity.

t: The true test of leadership is how well you function in a crisis.
x: Anyone can lead when things are calm; your real leadership shows in how steady and clear you are under pressure.

t: The key responsibility of leadership is to think about the future. No one else can do it for you.
x: Someone has to look ahead and plan for what is coming, and that job belongs to the leader.

t: The potential of the average person is like a huge ocean unsailed, a new continent unexplored, a world of possibilities waiting to be released and channeled toward some great good.
x: Ordinary people carry great untapped ability, and part of leading is helping release it for good ends.

t: A clear vision, backed by definite plans, gives you a tremendous feeling of confidence and personal power.
w: The Great Big Book of Wisdom
x: Knowing where you're going and how you'll get there gives you steady confidence to act and lead.

t: People who take a long view of their lives and careers always seem to make much better decisions about their time and activities than people who give very little thought to the future.
x: Thinking about where your choices lead over years helps you spend your time and energy more wisely today.

t: Leaders never use the word failure. They look upon setbacks as learning experiences.
x: Treating setbacks as lessons keeps you and your team learning instead of giving up after a hard result.

t: Leaders think and talk about the solutions. Followers think and talk about the problems.
x: Focusing conversation on solutions moves a team forward, while dwelling on problems tends to drain it.

t: The three 'C's' of leadership are consideration, caring, and courtesy. Be polite to everyone.
x: Simple courtesy and genuine care for people build goodwill that makes everything else in leading easier.

t: Practice Golden Rule Management in everything you do. Manage others the way you would like to be managed.
x: Treating people the way you would want to be treated is a reliable guide for managing and leading well.

t: Leaders set high standards. Refuse to tolerate mediocrity or poor performance.
x: Expecting excellence and lovingly addressing poor work shows people you believe they are capable of more.

t: Move out of your comfort zone. You can only grow if you are willing to feel awkward and uncomfortable when you try something new.
x: Growth almost always feels awkward at first, so discomfort is often a sign you're learning something new.

t: The future belongs to the competent. Get good, get better, be the best!
x: Steadily improving your skill is one of the surest ways to be useful to others and ready for what's ahead.

t: Your life only gets better when you get better.
x: Circumstances improve most reliably when you work on your own growth, character, and skills.

t: You are the architect of your own destiny; you are the master of your own fate; you are behind the steering wheel of your life.
w: The 21 Success Secrets of Self-Made Millionaires
x: Your choices shape the direction of your life, so take responsibility rather than waiting on circumstances.

t: Successful people are always looking for opportunities to help others. Unsuccessful people are always asking, "What's in it for me?"
x: A habit of helping others, rather than asking what's in it for you, builds lasting success and relationships.

t: The foundation of lasting self-confidence and self-esteem is excellence, mastery of your work.
w: The Great Big Book of Wisdom
x: Real confidence comes from becoming genuinely good at your work, not from positive feelings alone.

t: Entrepreneurial leadership requires the ability to move quickly when opportunity presents itself.
x: Opportunities often have a short window, so leaders need the readiness to decide and act promptly.

t: Respect is the key determinant of high-performance leadership. How much people respect you determines how well they perform.
x: People tend to give their best to leaders they respect, so earning respect directly affects a team's work.

t: The effective leader recognizes that they are more dependent on their people than they are on them. Walk softly.
x: Leaders rely on their people far more than the reverse, which calls for humility in how they treat them.

t: Leaders are innovative, entrepreneurial, and future-oriented. They focus on getting the job done.
x: Good leaders look ahead, try new approaches, and stay focused on actually getting important work done.

t: Always choose the future over the past. What do we do now?
x: Instead of dwelling on what went wrong, ask what to do next; that question moves people forward.

t: The best leaders have a high consideration factor. They really care about their people.
x: People can tell whether a leader truly cares about them, and that care builds loyalty and effort.

t: There are no limits to what you can accomplish, except the limits you place on your own thinking.
x: Often the biggest limit on what you achieve is how small you allow yourself to think.

t: Develop an attitude of gratitude. Say 'Thank you' to everyone you meet for everything they do for you.
x: Thanking people regularly and sincerely makes them feel valued and builds warmer relationships at work and home.

t: Optimism is the one quality more associated with success and happiness than any other.
x: A hopeful outlook helps you keep going through difficulty and lifts the people around you.

t: Make your life a masterpiece, imagine no limitations on what you can be, have, or do.
x: Picturing your life without self-imposed limits can help you aim higher with your gifts and time.

t: You have within you the potential to accomplish wonderful things with your life.
w: The 21 Success Secrets of Self-Made Millionaires
x: Each person carries real potential for good, which is a reason to keep growing and to believe in others.

t: Every minute spent in planning saves 10 minutes in execution.
x: A little planning up front saves a great deal of wasted effort, making your work days calmer and more effective.

t: Having a busy day and having a successful day are not synonymous.
x: Activity isn't the same as progress, so judge your day by what mattered most rather than by how full it was.

t: Determine that the thing can and shall be done, and then we shall find the way.
w: Speech in the House of Representatives (20 June 1848)
x: Big tasks yield to firm resolve; once you commit that something must happen, practical paths tend to appear.

t: Always bear in mind that your own resolution to succeed, is more important than any other one thing.
x: Talent and circumstance matter, but your own steady determination is the factor most within your control.

t: The leading rule for the lawyer, as for the man of every other calling, is diligence. Leave nothing for to-morrow which can be done to-day.
x: Diligence is the common rule of every calling; doing today's work today keeps small tasks from becoming burdens.

t: Resolve to be honest at all events; and if in your own judgment you cannot be an honest lawyer, resolve to be honest without being a lawyer.
x: Integrity comes before career; if a role would require dishonesty, it is the role that should go, not the honesty.

t: Let us have faith that right makes might, and in that faith, let us, to the end, dare to do our duty as we understand it.
x: Doing right is not always easy or rewarded at once, yet leaders are asked to act on conviction and trust that right will hold.

t: Upon the subject of education, not presuming to dictate any plan or system respecting it, I can only say that I view it as the most important subject which we as a people can be engaged in.
w: Address to the People of Sangamon County (9 March 1832)
x: Education shapes a people's future, which is why teaching remains one of the most important things a community does.

t: Far and away the best prize that life offers is the chance to work hard at work worth doing.
w: Labor Day Address, New York State Agricultural Association, Syracuse (7 September 1903)
x: Meaningful, demanding work is a gift, not a burden; the chance to labour at something worthwhile is itself a reward.

t: It is not the critic who counts, not the man who points out how the strong man stumbled, or where the doer of deeds could have done better.
x: Critics are easy to find; credit belongs to those who step forward, try, and risk failure in doing real work.

t: In short, in life, as in a football game, the principle to follow is: Hit the line hard; don't foul and don't shirk, but hit the line hard!
x: Play fair and give full effort: no cheating and no slacking, but meet hard things head-on.

t: Be practical as well as generous in your ideals. Keep your eyes on the stars, but remember to keep your feet on the ground.
w: Address at Prize Day, Groton School (24 May 1904)
x: Aim high, but stay practical; ideals only change things when they are joined to realistic, grounded action.

t: I don't pity any man who does hard work worth doing. I admire him. I pity the creature who does not work, at whichever end of the social scale he may regard himself as being.
w: Remarks to the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen, Chattanooga (8 September 1902)
x: Honest labour of any kind deserves respect, while idleness diminishes a person whatever their wealth or status.

t: We cannot avoid meeting great issues. All that we can determine for ourselves is whether we shall meet them well or ill.
x: We do not get to choose all our challenges; we do choose whether to face them with courage and care.

t: Be courteous to all, but intimate with few, and let those few be well tried before you give them your confidence; true friendship is a plant of slow growth.
x: Be kind to everyone but careful with trust; deep friendships are tested slowly and are worth the wait.

t: I hope I shall always possess firmness and virtue enough to maintain (what I consider the most enviable of all titles) the character of an honest man.
x: A good reputation for honesty is worth more than any title or honour a leader could be given.

t: It is better to offer no excuse than a bad one.
x: A weak excuse damages trust more than a plain admission; owning a failure is the better path.

t: Promote, then, as an object of primary importance, institutions for the general diffusion of knowledge.
x: A free and healthy society depends on spreading knowledge widely, which makes schools and teachers vital.

t: Discipline is the soul of an army. It makes small numbers formidable; procures success to the weak, and esteem to all.
w: Letter of Instructions to the Captains of the Virginia Regiments (29 July 1759)
x: Order and self-control let a small, ordinary group achieve far more than its size would suggest.

t: Never give in — never, never, never, never, in nothing great or small, large or petty, never give in except to convictions of honour and good sense.
x: Perseverance matters, but so does wisdom: hold firm on what matters while staying open to honour and good sense.

t: Courage is rightly esteemed the first of human qualities, because, as has been said, it is the quality which guarantees all others.
w: "Unlucky Alfonso", Collier's (27 June 1931); reprinted in Great Contemporaries (1937)
x: Without courage, other virtues fail under pressure; it is what lets honesty, kindness and loyalty hold when tested.

t: Personally, I am always ready to learn, although I do not always like being taught.
w: Speech in the House of Commons (4 November 1952)
x: Even strong leaders find correction uncomfortable; the goal is to keep learning anyway.

t: To improve is to change, so to be perfect is to have changed often.
w: Speech in the House of Commons (23 June 1925)
x: Growth requires change; those who improve most are willing to adjust again and again.

t: Every day you may make progress. Every step may be fruitful. Yet there will stretch out before you an ever-lengthening, ever-ascending, ever-improving path.
w: "Painting as a Pastime", The Strand Magazine (1921–22)
x: Steady daily effort compounds; there is always further to grow, which keeps work and learning fresh.

t: Where my reason, imagination or interest were not engaged, I would not or I could not learn.
x: Students learn best when their reason, imagination or interest is engaged, a reminder for every teacher and parent.

t: Resolution. Resolve to perform what you ought; perform without fail what you resolve.
w: Autobiography, Part II (list of thirteen virtues, 1784)
x: Make fewer promises to yourself, and keep the ones you make; character is built on follow-through.

t: Industry. Lose no time; be always employ'd in something useful; cut off all unnecessary actions.
w: Autobiography, Part II (list of thirteen virtues, 1784)
x: Time is a resource; using it on useful work and cutting waste makes room for what matters most.

t: Human felicity is produc'd not so much by great pieces of good fortune that seldom happen, as by little advantages that occur every day.
x: Happiness is built more from small daily kindnesses and habits than from rare windfalls.

t: From a child I was fond of reading, and all the little money that came into my hands was ever laid out in books.
x: A love of reading formed in childhood can shape a whole life; books are a wise place to spend what we have.

t: For my own Part, when I am employed in serving others, I do not look upon myself as conferring Favours, but as paying Debts.
x: Serving others is not a favour we grant but a debt we owe for all we have received.

t: The purpose of an organization is to enable common men to do uncommon things.
x: Good organisations let ordinary people achieve extraordinary results together, which is a test of any team or school.

t: A superior who works on his own development sets an almost irresistible example.
x: Leaders who keep growing themselves set an example that shapes their teams more than any instruction.

t: A man should never be appointed into a managerial position if his vision focuses on people's weaknesses rather than on their strengths.
x: Leaders should build on people's strengths; fixating on weaknesses drains a team and wastes talent.

t: Morale in an organization does not mean that "people get along together"; the test is performance not conformance.
x: Good morale is not just getting along; it shows in whether a team does excellent work together.

t: Effective executives do first things first and they do one thing at a time.
w: The Effective Executive, ch. 5 "First Things First" (1966)
x: Focus beats busyness: doing the most important thing first, one at a time, is how effective people get results.

t: What counts is not necessarily the size of the dog in the fight — it's the size of the fight in the dog.
w: Remarks at Republican National Committee Breakfast (31 January 1958)
x: Determination and heart often matter more than size or resources when facing a hard challenge.

t: Humility must always be the portion of any man who receives acclaim earned in blood of his followers and sacrifices of his friends.
x: Leaders who receive praise should stay humble, remembering the sacrifices others made to earn it.

t: The essence of leadership is to get others to do something because they think you want it done and because they know it is worth while doing.
w: Remarks at the Republican Campaign Picnic, Gettysburg Farm (12 September 1956)
x: Real leadership persuades people that the work is worth doing, rather than simply giving orders.

t: Leadership consists of nothing but taking responsibility for everything that goes wrong and giving your subordinates credit for everything that goes well.
w: Interview in Edgar F. Puryear Jr., Nineteen Stars (1971)
x: Good leaders take the blame when things go wrong and pass the credit to their team when things go well.

t: Plans are worthless, but planning is everything.
w: Remarks at the National Defense Executive Reserve Conference (14 November 1957)
x: Plans change once reality arrives, but the thinking done while planning prepares you to adapt well.

t: I learned the lesson that great men cultivate love, and that only little men cherish a spirit of hatred.
x: Hatred shrinks the person who holds it; greatness of character shows in choosing love instead.

t: I would permit no man, no matter what his colour might be, to narrow and degrade my soul by making me hate him.
x: Refusing to hate those who wrong us protects our own souls, even when bitterness would feel justified.

t: Few things help an individual more than to place responsibility upon him, and to let him know that you trust him.
x: Trusting people with real responsibility helps them grow; leaders and parents can give that gift.

t: I have learned that success is to be measured not so much by the position that one has reached in life as by the obstacles which he has overcome while trying to succeed.
x: Success is measured not only by where we end up but by the obstacles we overcome on the way.

t: Nothing ever comes to me, that is worth having, except as the result of hard work.
x: Worthwhile things rarely come easily; steady hard work is usually the price of what is worth having.

t: In meeting men, in many places, I have found that the happiest people are those who do the most for others; the most miserable are those who do the least.
x: Joy is closely tied to service; those who give most to others often find the deepest happiness.

t: If there is no struggle, there is no progress. Those who profess to favor freedom, and yet depreciate agitation, are men who want crops without plowing up the ground.
w: West India Emancipation speech, Canandaigua, New York (August 1857)
x: Real progress requires struggle; wanting good results without hard effort is like wanting a harvest without ploughing.

t: I would unite with anybody to do right; and with nobody to do wrong.
x: Work with anyone for a good cause, but never join anyone in doing wrong; cooperation has a moral limit.

t: You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.
w: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, ch. 10 (1845)
x: Courage and learning can restore a person's dignity, turning a story of oppression into one of freedom.

t: From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom.
w: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, ch. 6 (1845)
x: For Douglass, learning to read opened the way to freedom, a reminder of how much education can change a life.

t: My theory of self-made men is, then, simply this: that they are men of work.
w: Self-Made Men, address at Carlisle Indian Industrial School (c. 1893)
x: Behind most success lies plain, persistent work rather than luck or genius, which is encouraging for everyone.

t: Nothing valuable can be lost by taking time.
x: Under pressure, a pause to think rarely costs anything good, while haste can cost a great deal.

t: The dogmas of the quiet past are inadequate to the stormy present. The occasion is piled high with difficulty, and we must rise with the occasion.
x: Old habits may not fit new challenges; leaders must be willing to think freshly when circumstances change.

t: In this sad world of ours, sorrow comes to all; and, to the young, it comes with bitterest agony, because it takes them unawares.
x: Written to a grieving girl, it models gentle honesty about grief, especially for children meeting loss for the first time.

t: I shall try to correct errors when shown to be errors; and I shall adopt new views so fast as they shall appear to be true views.
x: Admitting mistakes and updating your views is a strength in a leader, not a weakness.

t: A sound body is good; a sound mind is better; but a strong and clean character is better than either.
w: Address at Prize Day, Groton School (24 May 1904)
x: Health and intellect matter, but character is what most deserves our effort as learners, parents and teachers.

t: Happiness can not come to any man capable of enjoying true happiness unless it comes as the sequel to duty well and honestly done.
w: Address at Prize Day, Groton School (24 May 1904)
x: Lasting contentment tends to follow faithful work and kept responsibilities rather than the chase for pleasure.

t: The same qualities that make a decent boy make a decent man. They have different manifestations, but fundamentally they are the same.
w: Address at Prize Day, Groton School (24 May 1904)
x: The habits children practise now are the character they will carry as adults, which is why small lessons matter.

t: It is hard to fail, but it is worse never to have tried to succeed. In this life we get nothing save by effort.
w: The Strenuous Life, speech to the Hamilton Club, Chicago (10 April 1899)
x: Failure hurts, but never trying costs more; growth comes only through effort that risks falling short.

t: A slender acquaintance with the world must convince every man, that actions, not words, are the true criterion of the attachment of his friends
w: Letter to Major-General John Sullivan (15 December 1779)
x: Loyalty shows in what people do, not what they say, and the same test applies to our own commitments.

t: Of all the dispositions and habits, which lead to political prosperity, Religion and Morality are indispensable supports.
x: Washington held that a free society rests on faith and moral character, not only on laws and institutions.

t: I hold the maxim no less applicable to public than to private affairs, that honesty is always the best policy.
x: The same honesty expected at home should guide public and professional life; integrity should not change with the setting.

t: Let us therefore animate and encourage each other, and show the whole world that a Freeman, contending for liberty on his own ground, is superior to any slavish mercenary on earth.
w: General Orders, Headquarters, New York (2 July 1776)
x: In hard moments, mutual encouragement is itself a form of leadership that strengthens a whole team.

t: I have nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears, and sweat.
w: First speech as Prime Minister, House of Commons (13 May 1940)
x: Honest leaders tell people the true cost of a hard task; candour builds more trust than false comfort.

t: Now this is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning.
w: Speech at the Lord Mayor's Luncheon, Mansion House, London (10 November 1942)
x: An early success is worth marking, but a long effort still lies ahead; perseverance means not mistaking a start for a finish.

t: The price of greatness is responsibility.
x: Influence and position bring obligations; the more we are given, the more we are answerable for.

t: Order. Let all your things have their places; let each part of your business have its time.
w: Autobiography, Part II (list of thirteen virtues, 1784)
x: Simple order in our things and our time frees attention for the work and people that matter most.

t: Sincerity. Use no hurtful deceit; think innocently and justly, and, if you speak, speak accordingly.
w: Autobiography, Part II (list of thirteen virtues, 1784)
x: Honest speech starts with honest thinking; what we say should match what we truly believe.

t: I grew convinc'd that truth, sincerity and integrity in dealings between man and man were of the utmost importance to the felicity of life
x: Franklin found by experience that trustworthy dealings are central to a happy life, not just a moral rule.

t: Whenever anything is being accomplished, it is being done, I have learned, by a monomaniac with a mission.
x: Great work usually needs someone single-minded enough to carry it, which shows the value of focused commitment.

t: To be a manager requires more than a title, a big office, and other outward symbols of rank. It requires competence and performance of a high order.
x: Authority is earned through competence and results, not through titles or the trappings of position.

t: A manager's task is to make the strengths of people effective and their weakness irrelevant - and that applies fully as much to the manager's boss as it applies to the manager's subordinates
x: Good leaders arrange work around people's strengths, and that generosity applies to their own bosses as well.

t: A people that values its privileges above its principles soon loses both.
x: When comfort is placed above conviction, both are eventually lost, in nations and in families alike.

t: I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important. The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.
w: Address to the World Council of Churches, Evanston (19 August 1954), quoting a former college president
x: Urgent demands can crowd out the important ones; wise people protect time for what truly matters.

t: As their heirs, may we never confuse honest dissent with disloyal subversion.
w: Speech at the Columbia University Bicentennial (31 May 1954)
x: Healthy teams and communities can tell honest disagreement apart from disloyalty, and make room for it.

t: No race can prosper till it learns that there is as much dignity in tilling a field as in writing a poem.
w: Up From Slavery, ch. 14, Atlanta Exposition Address (1901)
x: All honest work carries dignity, whether done with the hands or the mind, and deserves equal respect.

t: I have begun everything with the idea that I could succeed, and I never had much patience with the multitudes of people who are always ready to explain why one cannot succeed.
x: Hopeful determination opens doors that excuses keep shut; beginning with belief matters.

t: Perhaps the most valuable thing that I got out of my second year was an understanding of the use and value of the Bible.
x: A teacher's influence can be lifelong; for Washington, learning to love Scripture was the best fruit of school.

t: Power concedes nothing without a demand. It never did and it never will.
w: West India Emancipation speech, Canandaigua, New York (3 August 1857)
x: Injustice rarely corrects itself; it takes people willing to speak up and press for what is right.

t: I felt as I never felt before. It was a glorious resurrection, from the tomb of slavery, to the heaven of freedom.
w: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, ch. 10 (1845)
x: Standing up to oppression restored Douglass's spirit, showing how courage can renew a person from within.

t: Not transient and fitful effort, but patient, enduring, honest, unremitting and indefatigable work, into which the whole heart is put
x: Success comes less from bursts of effort than from steady, honest work done wholeheartedly over time.

t: Facts are stubborn things; and whatever may be our wishes, our inclinations, or the dictates of our passion, they cannot alter the state of facts and evidence
w: Argument in defence of the British soldiers, Boston Massacre trials (4 December 1770)
x: Good decisions start from facts rather than feelings; leaders must let evidence correct their preferences.

t: I must study Politicks and War that my sons may have liberty to study Mathematicks and Philosophy.
x: Parents often do hard, unglamorous work so their children can have wider opportunities; sacrifice can be a gift.

t: Let us tenderly and kindly cherish, therefore, the means of knowledge. Let us dare to read, think, speak, and write.
w: A Dissertation on the Canon and Feudal Law (1765)
x: Learning is to be cherished and used boldly; a free people needs the courage to read, think and speak.

t: I pray Heaven to bestow the best of blessings on this house and all that shall hereafter inhabit it. May none but honest and wise men ever rule under this roof.
x: Written on his first night in the White House, it is a prayer that any home or office be led with honesty and wisdom.

t: Whenever you are to do a thing, though it can never be known but to yourself, ask yourself how you would act were all the world looking at you, and act accordingly.
x: Character is what we do when no one is watching; a simple test is to act as if everyone could see.

t: Give up money, give up fame, give up science, give the earth itself and all it contains, rather than do an immoral act.
x: Written as advice to a teenage nephew, it places integrity above wealth, fame or achievement.

t: Encourage all your virtuous dispositions, and exercise them whenever an opportunity arises; being assured that they will gain strength by exercise, as a limb of the body does
x: Virtues grow with practice like muscles; small daily acts of goodness build habits that last.

t: Honesty is the first chapter in the book of wisdom.
x: Wisdom starts with honesty; cleverness without truthfulness leads people astray.

t: The great affairs of life are not performed by physical strength, or activity, or nimbleness of body, but by deliberation, character, expression of opinion.
w: On Old Age, ch. 6, trans. E. S. Shuckburgh
x: Wisdom and character, which can deepen with age, matter more for life's big tasks than speed or strength.

t: Such friendship enhances prosperity, and relieves adversity of its burden by halving and sharing it.
w: On Friendship, ch. 6, trans. E. S. Shuckburgh
x: True friends double our joys and halve our troubles, which makes investing in friendship worthwhile.

t: We are not born for ourselves alone, but our country claims a share of our being, and our friends a share
w: De Officiis, Book I, §22, trans. Walter Miller (1913)
x: Our lives are bound up with others; family, friends and community all have a rightful claim on us.

t: The better and more noble, therefore, the character with which a man is endowed, the more does he prefer the life of service to the life of pleasure.
w: De Officiis, Book III, §25, trans. Walter Miller (1913)
x: Noble character shows itself in choosing service over comfort, a mark of good leaders and parents alike.

t: God Almighty has set before me two great objects, the suppression of the Slave Trade and the Reformation of Manners.
w: Journal (28 October 1787), in The Life of William Wilberforce (1838)
x: A clear sense of calling can focus a whole life; Wilberforce pursued these two aims for decades.

t: Beat the world at its own best weapons. Let your love be more affectionate, your mildness less open to irritation, your diligence more laborious, your activity more wakeful and persevering.
x: Believers commend their faith best by outdoing others in love, patience and hard work.

t: Consider sweetness of temper and activity of mind, if they naturally belong to you, as talents of special worth and utility, for which you will have to give account.
x: Even our temperament is a gift to steward; a kind spirit and an active mind are talents to use well.

t: The future doesn't belong to the fainthearted; it belongs to the brave.
w: Address to the Nation on the Challenger Disaster (28 January 1986)
x: Spoken to grieving schoolchildren, it reminds us that progress needs courage even after painful loss.

t: Freedom is never more than one generation away from extinction. We didn't pass it on to our children in the bloodstream.
w: Address to the Phoenix Chamber of Commerce (30 March 1961)
x: Values are not inherited automatically; each generation must teach them deliberately to the next.

t: We have every right to dream heroic dreams. Those who say that we're in a time when there are not heroes, they just don't know where to look.
x: Everyday heroes are all around us in ordinary jobs and homes, if we learn to notice and honour them.

t: You know, if you just set out to be liked, you would be prepared to compromise on anything, wouldn't you, at any time? And you would achieve nothing!
w: Interview for the Press Association (3 May 1989)
x: Leaders who need to be liked above all lose their way; doing what is right sometimes costs popularity.

t: I started life with two great advantages: no money, and good parents.
x: Good parenting can outweigh material advantage; what children receive at home matters more than wealth.

t: Pennies don't fall from heaven, they have to be earned here on earth.
w: Speech at the Lord Mayor's Banquet (12 November 1979)
x: Provision comes through honest work; resources must be earned and handled with care, not assumed.

t: A happy lot is this: good inclinations of the soul, good desires, good actions.
x: Real good fortune is inward: a well-ordered heart, right desires and good deeds, which no market crash or bad week can take away.

t: Remember that everything is only opinion, and all opinion depends on the mind.
x: Much of what upsets you is your judgment about events, not the events themselves, so changing your view can change your day.

t: To put it in a few words: life is short; we must try to make the most of the present with sound judgment and justice.
x: Life is short, so spend the hour in front of you wisely and fairly rather than waiting for a better moment that may not come.

t: This is what a happy life consists of: to know thoroughly the true nature of everything, what its substance is and what its form; and with all your heart and soul always to do what is just and to speak the truth.
x: A good life comes from seeing things as they truly are, then wholeheartedly doing what is right and telling the truth.

t: Always keep your purpose and resolve free from all compulsion and necessity.
x: Hold to your chosen purpose freely; pressure from others or circumstances should not decide what kind of person you are.

t: Every person's happiness depends on themselves, yet look: your life is almost over, and while you show yourself no respect, you make your happiness depend on the minds and opinions of other people.
x: Making your happiness depend on what others think hands them control of your life; your worth rests on your own conduct.

t: Whenever you choose, you can withdraw into yourself and be at rest, free from all your business.
x: Peace is always available within; even in a busy day you can step back into your own mind and find calm.

t: To live happily is a power within the soul, when it stays indifferent toward things that are by nature indifferent.
x: Contentment comes from not being disturbed by things that are neither good nor bad in themselves, like money, status or comfort.

t: Let this be your only joy and your only comfort: to pass without pause from one kind, sociable act to the next, always keeping God in mind.
x: Joy can be found in moving from one act of kindness to the next while keeping God in mind throughout the day.

t: Death hangs over you: while you are still alive, while you still can, be good.
x: Death is near for everyone, so the time to be good is today, while you still can, not someday later.

t: Shrink your whole life down to the measure of one single action.
x: Treat your whole life with the focus of a single task: do each thing fully and well, one action at a time.

t: Wherever you happen to live, you can live well and happily there.
x: Circumstances do not decide whether you can live well; wherever you are placed, a good life is still within reach.

t: Kind actions and a holy disposition are the only fruit of this earthly life.
x: The lasting fruit of a life is kindness toward others and a reverent heart, not wealth or reputation.

t: Give yourself time to learn something good, and stop roaming and wandering back and forth.
x: Make time to learn something worthwhile, and stop drifting between distractions that leave you no wiser.

t: So keep yourself truly simple, good, sincere, serious, free from all showing off, a lover of justice, devout, kind, tender-hearted, and strong and ready to undertake anything that befits you.
x: A good person is simple, sincere and unpretentious, loves justice, is gentle, and is strong enough to carry hard duties.

t: So take the trouble to learn what your nature requires, and let nothing else distract you.
x: Work out what your nature and calling truly require of you, and refuse to be pulled off course by everything else.

t: To righteousness, in speaking the truth freely, and without ambiguity; and in doing all things justly and discreetly.
x: Justice means speaking the truth plainly and without spin, and acting fairly and wisely in every matter.

t: Let no one be able to say truthfully of you that you are not simple, sincere and open, or not good.
x: Live so that no one could honestly accuse you of being insincere, devious or unkind; let your character answer for you.

t: An angry face is completely against nature, and it is often the very face of those who are about to die.
x: Anger distorts the face and the self; a scowl is unnatural, a sign of something going wrong inside rather than strength.

t: Everything you hope to reach in the future you can enjoy and possess right now, if you do not deny yourself your own happiness.
x: The peace and goodness you hope to reach someday can be yours now, if you stop postponing them and choose them today.

t: Death is a cessation from the impression of the senses, the tyranny of the passions, the errors of the mind, and the servitude of the body.
x: Marcus pictures death as release from the pull of the senses, the tyranny of passions and the errors of the mind.

t: Stop arguing and talking about what the marks of a good person are, and actually be one.
x: Stop debating what makes a good person and simply be one; character shows in what you do, not what you discuss.

t: In the morning, when you find yourself unwilling to get up, tell yourself at once: I am getting up to do a human being's work.
x: When duty is hard to face in the morning, remember you are getting up to do the work you were made to do.

t: If anyone corrects me and shows me clearly that I am wrong in any opinion or action of mine, I will gladly change my mind.
x: A wise person welcomes correction; being shown your error is a gift, and changing your mind is a strength.

t: Let us do our best to persuade them; but if reason and justice lead you to it, do it anyway, however much they oppose it.
x: Try to persuade people, but if reason and justice demand an action, do the right thing even when others object.

t: What use is suspicion at all? Why should mistrustful thoughts and suspicion about the future trouble your mind at all?
x: Suspicion and worry about what might happen only disturb the mind; they rarely prevent anything and often poison trust.

t: When someone's wrongdoing offends you, immediately turn to yourself and consider how you are guilty of the same kind of thing.
x: When someone's fault annoys you, first ask where you fail in the same way; it softens judgment and makes you humbler.

t: Make it a habit, whenever you see anyone do anything, to ask yourself at once (if possible): What is this person's aim in doing this?
x: Train yourself to ask what a person is aiming at; understanding motives helps you respond wisely instead of reacting.

t: The time of a man's life is as a point; the substance of it ever flowing, the sense obscure; and the whole composition of the body tending to corruption.
x: Life is brief and fleeting, so do not cling to it or waste it; use the short span you have for what matters.

t: Within our power are opinion, aim, desire, aversion, and, in one word, whatever affairs are our own.
x: Only your judgments, aims, desires and choices are truly yours; focus your energy there rather than on what you cannot control.

t: When you set about any action, remind yourself of what nature the action is.
x: Before you start something, picture what it will really involve, so that its normal frustrations do not knock you off balance.

t: If it be his pleasure that you should enact a poor man, or a cripple, or a ruler, or a private citizen, see that you act it well.
x: Whatever role God gives you, rich or poor, leader or private citizen, your task is to play it well, not to choose it.

t: You must cultivate either your own reason or else externals; apply yourself either to things within or without you—that is, be either a philosopher or one of the mob.
x: You must decide what you are cultivating: either your inner character or outward things; you cannot fully serve both.

t: In our power are our thinking, our intentions, our desires, our decisions.
x: Your thoughts, intentions, desires and decisions are the part of life you truly govern, so guard them carefully.

t: In company, avoid a frequent and excessive mention of your own actions and dangers.
x: Avoid talking much about your own exploits; constant self-reference wearies others and feeds pride.

t: If you wish your children and your wife and your friends to live forever, you are foolish, for you wish things to be in your power which are not so, and what belongs to others to be your own.
x: Loving family and friends is right, but demanding they never die is demanding control you do not have; hold them gratefully.

t: When, therefore, anyone provokes you, be assured that it is your own opinion which provokes you.
x: Others cannot make you angry without your consent; it is your own judgment that turns an insult into an injury.

t: Never proclaim yourself a philosopher, nor make much talk among the ignorant about your principles, but show them by actions.
x: Do not announce your principles or lecture people about them; let your conduct quietly show what you believe.

t: If you encounter a handsome person, you will find continence the faculty needed; if pain, then fortitude; if reviling, then patience.
x: Every trial is a call for a specific virtue: temptation calls for self-control, pain for courage, insults for patience.

t: How long, then, will you delay to demand of yourself the noblest improvements, and in no instance to transgress the judgments of reason?
x: Stop putting off the effort to become better; there is no reason to wait to live by what you know is right.

t: If you ever happen to turn your attention to externals, for the pleasure of anyone, be assured that you have ruined your scheme of life.
x: The moment you shape your life around pleasing others, you have abandoned your own course and principles.

t: Let death and exile, and all other things which appear terrible, be daily before your eyes, but death chiefly; and you will never entertain an abject thought, nor too eagerly covet anything.
x: Keeping death in view daily cures petty thoughts and greedy cravings, and helps you live with seriousness and freedom.

t: If, then, you shun only those undesirable things which you can control, you will never incur anything which you shun; but if you shun sickness, or death, or poverty, you will run the risk of wretchedness.
x: If you only fear the wrongs you can avoid, like your own bad choices, you will not be crushed by what lies beyond you.

t: Great is the combat, divine is the work; it is for kingship, for freedom, for happiness, for freedom from perturbation.
x: The struggle for self-mastery is the noblest work there is, because it wins freedom, happiness and a calm mind.

t: When you are going to take in hand any act remind yourself what kind of an act it is.
x: Before acting, consider what kind of act it is, so you can meet its difficulties with a clear head.

t: Every habit and faculty is maintained and increased by the corresponding actions: the habit of walking by walking, the habit of running by running.
x: Habits grow by practice, good or bad; whatever you repeatedly do, you become better at and more inclined toward.

t: Have you taken pains to learn what is a good man and what is a bad man, and how a man becomes one or the other?
x: Before you can become a good person you need to understand what goodness is and how character is formed or lost.

t: Each man is improved and preserved by corresponding acts, the carpenter by acts of carpentry, the grammarian by acts of grammar.
x: Skill and character grow by doing: a carpenter improves by building, and a person grows in virtue by acting virtuously.

t: My man, first of all consider what kind of thing it is; and then examine your own nature, if you are able to sustain the character.
x: Before taking on a role, honestly weigh both what it demands and whether you have the strength to carry it.

t: If a man is unhappy, remember that his unhappiness is his own fault; for God has made all men to be happy, to be free from perturbations.
x: Epictetus taught that unhappiness flows from our own false judgments, since God made people capable of peace and contentment.
